```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(janeaustenr)
library(syuzhet)
library(sentimentr)
library(knitr)

accent   <- "#2a78d6"
accent_2 <- "#eb6834"
theme_sa <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot")
```

# Overview

This report has two halves. The first reproduces the sentiment analysis example from Chapter 2 of
*Text Mining with R*. The second extends it with a different corpus — five gothic novels — and two
additional lexicons, then asks how much the choice of lexicon changes the answer.

The short version of the finding: **it changes it completely.** On the gothic novels, one lexicon
says the books are negative and three say they are positive. The texts did not change; only the
dictionary did.

**Source of the original example:** Silge, J. and Robinson, D. (2017), *Text Mining with R: A Tidy
Approach*, O'Reilly Media. Chapter 2, "Sentiment analysis with tidy data". The code in Section 3
follows that chapter closely; any changes are noted where they occur.

## A note on where the lexicons come from

The chapter calls `tidytext::get_sentiments()`, which for `afinn` and `nrc` downloads the data
through the `textdata` package and asks the user to accept each lexicon's licence first. That
prompt cannot be answered in a document that renders automatically, so this report takes the same
three lexicons from the `syuzhet` package, which ships its own copies. `bing` still comes from
`tidytext` directly, exactly as in the book.

```{r}
#| label: lexicons
bing  <- get_sentiments("bing")
afinn <- as_tibble(get_sentiment_dictionary("afinn"))
nrc   <- as_tibble(get_sentiment_dictionary("nrc")) |>
  filter(lang == "english") |>
  select(word, sentiment) |>
  distinct()

tibble(
  lexicon = c("bing", "afinn", "nrc"),
  source  = c("tidytext", "syuzhet", "syuzhet"),
  entries = c(nrow(bing), nrow(afinn), nrow(nrc)),
  form    = c("positive / negative", "score from -5 to +5", "positive / negative + 8 emotions")
) |>
  kable()
```

# Reproducing the Book's Example

## Tidying the Austen novels

This is the chapter's code: one word per row, with line and chapter numbers kept so sentiment can
be tracked through each novel.

```{r}
#| label: tidy-austen
tidy_books <- austen_books() |>
  group_by(book) |>
  mutate(
    linenumber = row_number(),
    chapter = cumsum(str_detect(text, regex("^chapter [\\divxlc]", ignore_case = TRUE)))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

tibble(words = nrow(tidy_books), books = n_distinct(tidy_books$book)) |> kable()
```

## The joy words in *Emma*

The chapter's first result: the most common words in *Emma* that NRC labels as joy.

```{r}
#| label: joy
nrc_joy <- nrc |> filter(sentiment == "joy")

tidy_books |>
  filter(book == "Emma") |>
  inner_join(nrc_joy, by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10) |>
  kable()
```

This matches the book exactly: *good*, *young*, *friend*, *hope*, *happy*, *love*. It also shows the
method's weakness, which the authors point out — "young" is counted as joy, and "found" appears
because the lexicon cannot tell *found* the verb from *found* meaning established.

## Comparing the three lexicons on *Pride and Prejudice*

```{r}
#| label: three-lexicons
pride_prejudice <- tidy_books |> filter(book == "Pride & Prejudice")

afinn_pp <- pride_prejudice |>
  inner_join(afinn, by = "word") |>
  group_by(index = linenumber %/% 80) |>
  summarise(sentiment = sum(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(method = "AFINN")

bing_and_nrc <- bind_rows(
  pride_prejudice |>
    inner_join(bing, by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    mutate(method = "Bing et al."),
  pride_prejudice |>
    inner_join(nrc |> filter(sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative")),
               by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    mutate(method = "NRC")
) |>
  count(method, index = linenumber %/% 80, sentiment) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(sentiment = positive - negative)

comparison <- bind_rows(afinn_pp, bing_and_nrc |> select(index, sentiment, method))

comparison |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(
    chunks        = n(),
    mean          = round(mean(sentiment), 1),
    lowest        = min(sentiment),
    highest       = max(sentiment),
    pct_positive  = round(100 * mean(sentiment > 0)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Method", "Chunks", "Mean", "Lowest", "Highest", "% chunks positive"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-three-lexicons
#| fig-cap: "Sentiment through Pride and Prejudice, measured three ways. Each bar is a chunk of 80 lines."
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(comparison, aes(index, sentiment, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~method, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("AFINN" = accent, "Bing et al." = accent_2, "NRC" = "#1baf7a")) +
  labs(title = "The same novel, three lexicons, three different pictures",
       x = "Index (80 lines of text per chunk)", y = "Net sentiment") +
  theme_sa
```

The reproduction holds up. The three lines move together — they find the same peaks and troughs in
the same places — but they sit at different heights. NRC is the most positive, calling
`r comparison |> filter(method == "NRC") |> summarise(round(100*mean(sentiment>0))) |> pull()`% of
chunks positive, against
`r comparison |> filter(method == "Bing et al.") |> summarise(round(100*mean(sentiment>0))) |> pull()`%
for Bing. The book attributes this to the lexicons' own balance, and that is exactly what the
counts show:

```{r}
#| label: balance
bind_rows(
  bing |> count(sentiment) |> mutate(lexicon = "bing"),
  nrc |> filter(sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative")) |> count(sentiment) |> mutate(lexicon = "nrc"),
  afinn |> mutate(sentiment = if_else(value > 0, "positive", "negative")) |> count(sentiment) |>
    mutate(lexicon = "afinn")
) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(pct_positive = round(100 * positive / (positive + negative), 1)) |>
  select(lexicon, negative, positive, pct_positive) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Lexicon", "Negative words", "Positive words", "% positive"))
```

NRC is 41% positive while Bing is only 29.5%, so NRC scores any text higher. Nothing about the
novel causes that difference.

## Words that drive the score

```{r}
#| label: fig-contributors
#| fig-cap: "Words contributing most to positive and negative sentiment across all six Austen novels (Bing)."
#| fig-height: 4
tidy_books |>
  inner_join(bing, by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  count(word, sentiment, sort = TRUE) |>
  group_by(sentiment) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 10) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(word = reorder(word, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, word, fill = sentiment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~sentiment, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(negative = accent_2, positive = accent)) +
  labs(title = "Top sentiment words in the Austen novels", x = "Occurrences", y = NULL) +
  theme_sa
```

The chapter uses this plot to make a point about error-checking, and the point survives: **"miss"**
is counted as negative 1,855 times, but in Austen it is almost always a title for an unmarried
woman, not a failure. In the book the authors add it to a custom stop-word list. I leave it in here
so the problem stays visible, and return to it in the conclusions.

# Extension 1: A Different Corpus

## The gothic novels

I kept the method and changed the material: five gothic and horror novels from Project Gutenberg,
chosen because the genre should sit at the opposite emotional end from Austen's social comedies.

```{r}
#| label: load-gothic
gothic <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/main/Week10A/data/gothic_books.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

tidy_gothic <- gothic |>
  group_by(title) |>
  mutate(linenumber = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

tidy_gothic |>
  count(title, name = "words") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Novel", "Words"))
```

The corpus was downloaded once with `gutenbergr` and saved to my repository, so this document does
not depend on a live download. (One title, an older edition of *Frankenstein*, had been archived on
the mirror and was replaced with Gutenberg ID 84.)

## Does the method separate the genres?

```{r}
#| label: genre-chunks
chunk_sentiment <- function(tokens, group_col) {
  tokens |>
    inner_join(bing, by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    count(.data[[group_col]], index = linenumber %/% 80, sentiment) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
    mutate(net = positive - negative)
}

austen_lines <- austen_books() |>
  group_by(book) |>
  mutate(linenumber = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

gothic_chunks <- chunk_sentiment(tidy_gothic, "title")
austen_chunks <- chunk_sentiment(austen_lines, "book")

bind_rows(
  austen_chunks |> group_by(work = as.character(book)) |>
    summarise(corpus = "Austen", .groups = "drop_last",
              chunks = n(), mean_net = round(mean(net), 1),
              pct_positive = round(100 * mean(net > 0))) |> ungroup(),
  gothic_chunks |> group_by(work = title) |>
    summarise(corpus = "Gothic", .groups = "drop_last",
              chunks = n(), mean_net = round(mean(net), 1),
              pct_positive = round(100 * mean(net > 0))) |> ungroup()
) |>
  select(corpus, work, chunks, mean_net, pct_positive) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Corpus", "Work", "Chunks", "Mean net sentiment", "% chunks positive"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-genres
#| fig-cap: "Net sentiment per 80-line chunk (Bing). Every Austen novel sits above zero; every gothic novel sits below it."
#| fig-height: 3.6
bind_rows(
  austen_chunks |> transmute(corpus = "Austen", net),
  gothic_chunks |> transmute(corpus = "Gothic", net)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = net, fill = corpus)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.55, color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Austen = accent, Gothic = accent_2), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Bing separates the two genres cleanly",
       x = "Net sentiment per 80-line chunk", y = "Density") +
  theme_sa +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Using Bing, the separation is complete: all six Austen novels average positive (+7.3 to +12.1) and
all five gothic novels average negative (−1.6 to −8.3). *Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde* is the darkest, with
only 16% of its chunks positive, against 86% for *Persuasion*.

# Extension 2: Additional Lexicons

I added two more, each chosen for a different reason.

**The syuzhet lexicon** is a fourth word-level dictionary, developed by Matthew Jockers for
narrative analysis and bundled with the `syuzhet` package. It is the largest of the four, so it
tests whether a bigger dictionary changes the answer.

**`sentimentr`** is not a word list but a different method. It scores whole sentences and applies
*valence shifters*: negators, amplifiers and de-amplifiers. This matters because every lexicon used
so far is blind to the word "not".

```{r}
#| label: sentimentr-demo
tibble(sentence = c("This is very good.", "This is not good at all.")) |>
  mutate(sentimentr_score = map_dbl(sentence, ~ sentiment_by(get_sentences(.x))$ave_sentiment),
         bing_words = c("good = positive", "good = positive")) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Sentence", "sentimentr", "What a word lexicon sees"))
```

## How often does negation actually occur?

Before assuming negation matters, it is worth measuring.

```{r}
#| label: negation
negators <- c("not", "no", "never", "without", "none", "cannot", "nor", "neither", "nothing")

bigrams <- gothic |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(text = paste(text, collapse = " "), .groups = "drop") |>
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n = 2) |>
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ", fill = "right")

all_matches <- bigrams |> inner_join(bing, by = c("word2" = "word"), relationship = "many-to-many")
negated     <- all_matches |> filter(word1 %in% negators)

n_matches <- nrow(all_matches)
n_negated <- nrow(negated)

tibble(
  sentiment_words = n_matches,
  negated_words   = n_negated,
  pct             = round(100 * n_negated / n_matches, 2)
) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Sentiment words", "Directly preceded by a negator", "%"))
```

```{r}
#| label: negation-examples
negated |>
  filter(sentiment == "positive") |>
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8) |>
  mutate(counted_as = "positive", should_be = "negative") |>
  kable(col.names = c("Negator", "Word", "Times", "Counted as", "Should be"))
```

About 2% of sentiment words in the gothic corpus are directly negated, and "not like", "no good"
and "not love" are all scored as positive by every word-level lexicon here. It is a real error, but
a small one — too small to explain the differences that follow.

## All four lexicons, both corpora

```{r}
#| label: four-lexicons
syuzhet_lex <- as_tibble(get_sentiment_dictionary("syuzhet"))

both <- bind_rows(
  tidy_gothic |> transmute(corpus = "Gothic", word),
  austen_lines |> transmute(corpus = "Austen", word)
)

lexicon_scores <- bind_rows(
  both |> inner_join(bing, by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    group_by(corpus) |> summarise(lexicon = "bing",
      score = mean(if_else(sentiment == "positive", 1, -1)), matched = n(), .groups = "drop"),
  both |> inner_join(afinn, by = "word") |>
    group_by(corpus) |> summarise(lexicon = "afinn", score = mean(value), matched = n(), .groups = "drop"),
  both |> inner_join(nrc |> filter(sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative")),
                     by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    group_by(corpus) |> summarise(lexicon = "nrc",
      score = mean(if_else(sentiment == "positive", 1, -1)), matched = n(), .groups = "drop"),
  both |> inner_join(syuzhet_lex, by = "word") |>
    group_by(corpus) |> summarise(lexicon = "syuzhet", score = mean(value), matched = n(), .groups = "drop")
)

lexicon_scores |>
  select(lexicon, corpus, score) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = corpus, values_from = score) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)),
         gothic_sign = if_else(Gothic < 0, "negative", "positive")) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Lexicon", "Austen", "Gothic", "Gothic verdict"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-four
#| fig-cap: "Mean sentiment per matched word. Austen is positive on every lexicon; the gothic novels are not."
#| fig-height: 3.4
lexicon_scores |>
  ggplot(aes(x = score, y = lexicon, fill = corpus)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey40") +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", score)), position = position_dodge(width = 0.7),
            hjust = ifelse(lexicon_scores$score < 0, 1.2, -0.2), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Austen = accent, Gothic = accent_2), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
  labs(title = "Three of four lexicons call the gothic novels positive",
       x = "Mean sentiment per matched word", y = NULL) +
  theme_sa +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

**This is the main result of the extension.** On the same five novels, `bing` returns −0.087, a
negative verdict, while `nrc` returns +0.105, `afinn` +0.054 and `syuzhet` +0.036, all positive. The
earlier chunk-based chart made the gothic novels look decisively dark, but that conclusion came from
one lexicon, and three others disagree with it.

Why? Because `bing` is the harshest dictionary, only 29.5% positive, while NRC is 41% positive. A
lexicon's own balance sets a baseline, and texts are scored relative to it.

## Coverage: how much of the text each lexicon can even see

```{r}
#| label: coverage
coverage <- function(dictionary_words, tokens, label) {
  tibble(lexicon = label,
         matched = sum(tokens$word %in% dictionary_words),
         pct     = round(100 * mean(tokens$word %in% dictionary_words), 1))
}

bind_rows(
  coverage(bing$word, tidy_gothic, "bing"),
  coverage(afinn$word, tidy_gothic, "afinn"),
  coverage(unique(nrc$word), tidy_gothic, "nrc"),
  coverage(syuzhet_lex$word, tidy_gothic, "syuzhet")
) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Lexicon", "Words matched", "% of the corpus scored"))
```

Even the most generous lexicon scores only about 12% of the words, and Bing and AFINN see about 7%.
Every conclusion above therefore rests on roughly one word in ten; the other nine are invisible to
the method.

## sentimentr, which reads sentences

```{r}
#| label: sentimentr-books
sentimentr_scores <- bind_rows(
  gothic |> group_by(work = title) |> summarise(text = paste(text, collapse = " "), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(corpus = "Gothic"),
  austen_books() |> group_by(work = as.character(book)) |>
    summarise(text = paste(text, collapse = " "), .groups = "drop") |> mutate(corpus = "Austen")
) |>
  mutate(sentimentr = map_dbl(text, ~ sentiment_by(get_sentences(.x))$ave_sentiment)) |>
  select(corpus, work, sentimentr)

sentimentr_scores |>
  mutate(sentimentr = round(sentimentr, 3)) |>
  arrange(corpus, sentimentr) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Corpus", "Work", "sentimentr score"))
```

`sentimentr` agrees with the majority: the Austen novels score clearly higher (+0.086 to +0.114)
than the gothic ones (−0.020 to +0.037), but only *Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde* comes out negative. Adding
negation handling moved the gothic novels slightly, not decisively — which is consistent with
negation affecting only 2% of matches.

# Conclusions

- **The reproduction works.** The Chapter 2 code runs as published and gives the same results: the
  joy words in *Emma*, the three sentiment trajectories through *Pride and Prejudice*, and the
  observation that NRC runs more positive than Bing.
- **The lexicons agree on shape but not on level.** Across *Pride and Prejudice* all three find the
  same peaks and troughs. What differs is where zero sits, and that is set by each dictionary's own
  positive/negative balance rather than by the text.
- **On a new corpus, that difference becomes decisive.** Bing calls the five gothic novels negative
  (−0.087 per word); NRC, AFINN and syuzhet all call them positive. Austen is positive under every
  lexicon, so the method works where the signal is strong, and breaks down where it is marginal. If
  I had used a single lexicon and reported "gothic novels are dark", I would have been reporting a
  property of Bing.
- **Negation is a real but minor flaw.** Only 2.16% of sentiment words are directly negated, and
  `sentimentr`, which handles negation and intensifiers, mostly agrees with the simple word counts.
  Context errors are a bigger problem than negation: "miss" alone is counted negative 1,855 times in
  Austen, where it is a form of address.
- **Coverage is the limitation nobody mentions.** These lexicons score 7–12% of the words. A
  sentiment score is a summary of a small, non-random slice of the text, and comparisons across
  lexicons are partly comparisons of which slice each one happens to see.

**What I would do next.** The honest way to use these tools is to run at least two lexicons and
report the disagreement rather than picking the one that gives the expected answer. For the gothic
corpus specifically, a domain-appropriate dictionary — or a labelled sample of sentences to validate
against — would settle the question that four general-purpose lexicons could not.

# References

- Silge, J. and Robinson, D. (2017), *Text Mining with R: A Tidy Approach*, O'Reilly Media,
  Chapter 2, "Sentiment analysis with tidy data". The base example in Section 3 follows this
  chapter.
- Hu, M. and Liu, B. (2004), opinion lexicon ("bing"), supplied with `tidytext`.
- Nielsen, F. Å. (2011), AFINN word list; Mohammad, S. and Turney, P. (2013), NRC Emotion Lexicon;
  Jockers, M. (2015), syuzhet lexicon — all three accessed through the `syuzhet` package.
- Rinker, T. (2021), `sentimentr`: calculating text polarity sentiment at the sentence level with
  valence shifters.
- Corpus: *Dracula*, *Frankenstein*, *The Picture of Dorian Gray*, *The Turn of the Screw* and
  *The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde*, from Project Gutenberg via `gutenbergr`.
